% NOTE ON THE DOSE AXIS: the shutter was operated by hand, so its
% opening is recovered from the spectra to within one 0.1 s frame.
% The detected onset is an UPPER BOUND on the true shutter time and
% every absolute dose inherits that bound. The beam geometry is not
% in doubt: it was opened to the size of the chip, 50 x 50 um, and
% the supplied RADDOSE-3D run models exactly that. The 20 x 20 um
% figure elsewhere in the methods belongs to the time-resolved
% diffraction experiment.
%

% ---------------- METHODS ----------------

\subsubsection{Spectroscopy}

DTNB soaked R37S crystals were loaded into an EVAL film sandwich as shown in
\ref{fig:thinfilm} and described in \parencite{axford2016thinfilms,
JAHO2024fixedtarget}. The thin film sandwich was mounted on the beamline
goniometer using a tweezer pin; each region of the film was initially aligned
using the OAV so that it was coincident with the X-ray beam, and then rotated
45\(^{\circ}\) so that the crystal slurry was aligned with the UV-Vis
spectrometer optics. Spectra were recorded on an Andor SR303i spectrograph
fitted with a DU970P electron-multiplying CCD, using a 150 l mm\(^{-1}\)
grating blazed at 300 nm and a 100 \(\mu\)m entrance slit. Each spectrum
comprised five accumulations of 20 ms, and spectra were acquired as a kinetics
series with a cycle time of 0.1 s for 1000 cycles, giving 100 s of continuous
acquisition per film position. Because the probe beam samples a region of the
thin film rather than a single crystal, each measurement is an ensemble over
several randomly oriented microcrystals together with the surrounding mother
liquor; the random orientation is advantageous, as it averages out the
orientation dependent absorbance that complicates single crystal
\textit{in crystallo} spectroscopy. Five film positions were recorded for each
condition. Cryocooled measurements were made on single crystals at 100 K, with
single accumulated spectra recorded before irradiation and after each
successive X-ray exposure.

Absorbed X-ray dose was estimated using RADDOSE-3D
\parencite{dickerson2024doses}. Since the X-ray beam could not be matched
accurately to the footprint of the spectrometer probe, it was instead opened to
the dimensions of the chip, giving a 50 \(\times\) 50 \(\mu\)m top hat profile
at 5 \(\times\) 10\(^{12}\) ph s\(^{-1}\); the probed volume therefore sits
within a uniformly illuminated field, and a single whole crystal average dose is
an appropriate axis. The average whole crystal dose for a 0.1 s exposure at full
beam was 0.104 MGy, giving a dose rate of 1.042 MGy s\(^{-1}\) at
100 \% transmission, and dose was taken to accumulate linearly with elapsed
time and to scale with the nominal attenuator transmission.

Spectra were analysed using custom Python code (crystalspec), which reads the
raw Andor output directly and regenerates every figure and table presented here
in a single pass. Three properties of the data determined the analysis. First,
the absorbance of a microcrystal thin film is dominated by scattering rather
than by absorption, and the scattering magnitude varied by a factor of two to
four between film positions within a single condition; absolute absorbances
were therefore never averaged across positions. Second, mother liquor is
present in the probe path and contributes 20 to 27 \% of the raw absorbance
(Figure \ref{fig:spec_buffer}), so absolute absorbance carries a solvent
contribution that cannot be separated from the crystalline one. Third, the
crystalline volume fraction within the beam is unknown and varies between
positions, and consequently no amplitude reported here has been converted to a
concentration or to an absolute TNB occupancy.

Each spectrum was therefore expressed as a difference against the mean of the
first five frames recorded at that same film position, before irradiation. A
scattering background of the form
\(A_{\mathrm{scatter}}(\lambda) = c(\lambda/500)^{-n} + b\) was then fitted over
470--725 nm, a region in which neither TNB, DTNB nor the protein absorbs, and
subtracted across the full spectral range. Held out cross validation, in which
the background was fitted over 500--725 nm and its prediction tested against the
withheld 470--500 nm region, showed that a power law described the scattering
better than either a linear or a constant background (median residuals of
0.0056 and 0.0060 against 0.0122 absorbance units respectively), but
distinguished only weakly between exponents. The exponent was accordingly fixed
at \(n = 3\); allowing it to float produced values that ran to the imposed
bounds for a fifth of the DTNB spectra and a third of the apo spectra. No
smoothing was applied at any stage, since smoothing suppresses genuine peak
amplitudes and can introduce apparent shoulders.

Acquisition was started manually a short interval before the X-ray shutter was
opened, and that interval was not recorded. Since dose accumulates only while
the shutter is open, and since a fixed interval of time corresponds to a larger
absorbed dose at higher transmission, the start of irradiation was recovered
from the data for each trace individually. It was taken as the earliest frame at
which any spectral region departed persistently from its initial level, a
departure being required to exceed six times the local noise for three
consecutive frames. Detection across all regions rather than a single band is
necessary because the response is not simultaneous across the spectrum: the
300--325 nm band develops slowly at low dose rate and, used alone, indicated an
onset approximately 10 s after irradiation had demonstrably begun at
5 \% transmission. Recovered onsets were 3.2 to 6.4 s across the nine
conditions and showed no systematic dependence on transmission, consistent with
a manually operated shutter. Dose was accumulated from the recovered onset, and
the five frames immediately preceding it were averaged to form the dark
reference. Because the onset can only be detected once a change has become
measurable, it is properly an upper bound on the true shutter time, and the
absolute dose scale should be read as an estimate.

Exposures were continued deliberately until the sample was visibly damaged.
Beyond that point a trace continues to be recorded but no longer constitutes a
measurement of absorbance, since the optical path itself has changed. Loss of
optical integrity was identified using the 600--700 nm region, in which no
component of the system absorbs. The change observed there at high dose rate is
featureless, varying by less than 0.001 absorbance units between 575 and 700 nm,
and is therefore attributable to bulk opacity arising from bubble formation and
fracture rather than to any chromophore; it should be noted that this test
excludes a discrete absorption band and not a hypothetical structureless
absorber, which would be indistinguishable from opacity by this criterion.
Frames beyond the first sustained excursion exceeding 0.03 absorbance units in
this region were excluded. This assessment was made before scatter correction,
as the power law fit would otherwise absorb the broadband offset by which the
damage is recognised.

The detector baseline was reset periodically during acquisition to counteract
upward drift, which appears in the data as a step displacing the whole spectrum
between consecutive frames. Such steps were detected as changes in the mean
absorbance over 500--650 nm exceeding 0.01 absorbance units between successive
frames, a threshold approximately thirty times the frame to frame noise of
3.2 \(\times\) 10\(^{-4}\) determined from the conditions in which no resets
occurred. Isolated resets were removed by subtracting the wavelength resolved
offset across the step from all subsequent frames. Where resets arrived in
bursts, defined as three or more within 2 s, the trace was no longer treated as
a continuous measurement of a single sample state and the analysis window was
ended at the onset of the burst. Reset counts, stitching and truncation points
are given for every film position in Table \ref{tab:spec_qc} and illustrated in
Figure \ref{fig:spec_qc}.

Two conventions govern how film positions were combined, and they are not
interchangeable. For the permutation test all five positions in each arm
contribute, the test statistic being the difference signal integrated over the
dose range common to both arms. For dose resolved traces and endpoint values the
contributing set was instead held fixed at the three positions surviving
longest, so that a position dropping out part way through a series cannot
introduce a step into the mean of the remainder; an earlier version, in which
the mean was taken over whatever positions remained valid at each frame,
produced a spurious step of 0.0073 absorbance units, twenty six times the frame
to frame noise, at the dose where one position ended.

Absorbance was read at six fixed wavelengths, following the established
presentation for microspectrophotometry of irradiated crystals
\parencite{weik2002specific, sutton2013insights}: 310 nm, where a positive
feature grows in both soak states; 328 nm, the reported absorbance of the
protein--S--S--TNB mixed disulphide; 400 nm, assigned to the disulphide radical
anion; 412 nm, the free TNB\(^{2-}\) thiolate; 480 nm, an isosbestic point
reported for irradiated lysozyme and used here as a check; and 580 nm, assigned
to the solvated electron. Reading fixed wavelengths in preference to fitting
band centres was a deliberate choice. Frame to frame noise rises
forty eight fold from the 470--500 nm internal null into the 285--300 nm region,
and an earlier attempt to fit Gaussian band centres in the growth region
returned a DTNB minus apo shift that collapsed from \(-8.1\) to \(-1.4\) nm as
the lower limit of the fit window was moved from 292 to 304 nm; that shift, and
the interpretation of it in terms of disulphide dihedral angle, are therefore
not reported. The TNB signal was additionally integrated over 395--430 nm and
divided by the window width, since the 412 nm solution maximum is not resolved
\textit{in crystallo} but appears as a shoulder on a substantially larger
feature near 330--345 nm. Two further windows were integrated in parallel:
300--325 nm, which gains absorbance under irradiation, and 470--500 nm, which
should remain at zero after scatter correction and therefore serves as an
internal null.

Uncertainties were obtained by percentile bootstrap over film positions,
resampling the unit of replication rather than assuming normality, and
significance was assessed by exact permutation over all 252 possible five
against five splits. Dose response was summarised in two ways: as the initial
slope of the integrated signal against absorbed dose over a low dose window
common to every condition, and by fitting
\(A = A_{0} + B\exp(-D/d_{1})\) at each diagnostic wavelength
\parencite{sutton2013insights}. The 412 nm traces are not monotonic, each
falling to an extremum within the first few MGy and then returning partway
towards its starting value; the exponential was therefore fitted to the falling
segment alone, and the recovery is reported separately rather than folded into a
rate.

% ---------------- RESULTS ----------------

\subsubsection{Spectroscopy}

The initial spectra of DTNB soaked crystals show a broad absorbance maximum near
330--345 nm with a shoulder extending through 412 nm, the reported maximum for
TNB in solution. Contributions are expected from TNB, from unreacted DTNB near
330 nm, and from the protein itself below 300 nm, including the disulphide
absorbance near 260 nm \parencite{faraj2019cysreactivity}. Two features of the
configuration bound what can be asked of these data. The 412 nm band is not
resolved from the larger feature at shorter wavelength, so the analysis was
conducted in difference space throughout. More restrictively, no usable signal
exists below approximately 300 nm: absorbance falls from 0.28 at 300--350 nm to
0.12 at 180--220 nm in crystal and in mother liquor alike, which cannot occur if
light is reaching the detector, and the frame to frame noise in that region is
fifteen times that at 412 nm. The disulphide \(n \rightarrow \sigma^{*}\)
absorption near 250--260 nm is therefore not accessible. This reflects the
optical configuration rather than any limitation of the method, and suggests
that a UV transmitting mount, a UV blazed grating and a lower centre wavelength
would bring the disulphide itself within reach.

Referencing each film position to its own pre-irradiation state reveals a
reproducible response to irradiation (Figure \ref{fig:spec_spectra}). In both
DTNB soaked and unlabelled crystals a positive feature grows near 310 nm as dose
accumulates. This feature is the largest change in the spectrum, between two and
eleven times the magnitude of the label signal depending on dose rate, and since
it appears in both arms
it must be attributed to radiation chemistry of the protein rather than to the
label; it also overlies 328 nm, which is the reason the mixed disulphide cannot
be followed directly. In the DTNB soaked crystals, and not in the matched
controls, this is accompanied by a negative feature spanning approximately
370--450 nm and overlapping the TNB band. Integrated over 395--430 nm, the
endpoint difference between soaked and unlabelled films is \(-0.035\) at
5 \% transmission, \(-0.042\) at 25 \%, \(-0.019\) at 50 \% and \(-0.024\) at
100 \% (Table \ref{tab:spec_diagnostic}).

Reading the six diagnostic wavelengths (Figure \ref{fig:spec_diagnostic}) makes
the selectivity of this loss explicit. At 412 nm the DTNB minus apo difference is
negative at every transmission setting, whereas at 328 nm it changes sign between
settings, at \(-0.009\), \(-0.058\), \(+0.014\) and \(+0.019\), and no setting
excludes zero. The 480 nm and 580 nm channels remain within 0.007 of zero
throughout, as expected if neither an isosbestic point nor a solvated electron
population contributes appreciably at these dose rates. It is therefore the
412 nm channel alone that carries a consistent label specific signal, and the
mixed disulphide absorbance at 328 nm is masked by the protein growth beneath it.

The sign of the 412 nm signal separates the two soak states at every dose rate
examined. Comparing the dose integrated 395--430 nm signal between DTNB soaked
and matched unlabelled films, all five DTNB positions fall below all five control
positions at each of 5 \%, 25 \%, 50 \% and 100 \% transmission, giving in every
case the smallest attainable exact permutation probability for a five against
five comparison (\(p = 0.0079\), \(p = 0.032\) after Bonferroni correction for
four comparisons), with effect sizes of \(d = -1.6\), \(-2.5\), \(-2.7\) and
\(-1.6\) respectively. Complete separation at all four levels is the strongest
result this design can return: with five positions per group the permutation null
contains 252 splits, so no arrangement of these data could yield a smaller
probability. It should be emphasised that this result rests on the sign of the
change being consistent within each arm rather than on the amplitudes being
reproducible. The position to position standard deviation of the endpoint
difference within the DTNB arm, at 0.010 to 0.029 absorbance units, is comparable
to the difference between arms itself, as expected when the crystalline volume
fraction in the probed footprint varies between positions.

Comparison at the two highest dose rates is nevertheless made over a much shorter
dose range than at the two lowest, since exclusion of optically compromised
frames leaves only about 2 MGy of usable data at 50 \% and 100 \% transmission
against 5 and 23 MGy at 5 \% and 25 \%. The separation at high dose rate is
therefore established over the early part of the response only, and the
100 \% transmission result should be read as corroborating the others rather
than as an independent replicate.

The loss of TNB absorbance is dose dependent and saturates early. Fitted over the
first 2 MGy, a window accessible in every condition, the initial slope of the
395--430 nm signal against absorbed dose is negative in all four DTNB conditions,
at \(-0.0025\), \(-0.0071\), \(-0.0036\) and \(-0.0054\) per MGy at 5, 25, 50 and
100 \% transmission, and positive in the unlabelled controls at the three lower
dose rates, at \(+0.0025\), \(+0.0020\) and \(+0.0025\) per MGy at 5, 10 and
25 \%. The inversion of sign with soak state is the clearest expression of the
effect and requires no kinetic model. Fitting a single exponential to the
difference between the labelled and unlabelled traces at 412 nm gives
\(D_{90}\), the dose at which nine tenths of the loss has occurred, of 1.70,
9.51 and 0.80 MGy at 5, 25 and 50 \% transmission (\(R^{2} = 0.92\) to 0.99;
Table \ref{tab:spec_D90}). The label specific chemistry is therefore
substantially complete while the measurement is still in progress, which is what
the consumption of a finite accessible pool of mixed disulphide would produce.

At 100 \% transmission the same fit does not determine a rate, and \(D_{90}\)
is reported only as a lower bound of 1.9 MGy. The reason is not the quality of
the data but the range over which they were collected: the film fails optically
at 2.1 MGy, and an exponential is close to linear over the first fraction of its
own characteristic dose, so a curve that has barely begun to bend admits time
constants spanning orders of magnitude at indistinguishable goodness of fit. The
quantity that exposes this is the fraction of the modelled decay traversed by
the measurement, \(1 - \exp(-D_{\mathrm{max}}/d_{1})\), which is 0.999, 0.996
and 0.998 at the three lower settings but 0.140 at 100 \%. Profiling the
characteristic dose at that setting, with the remaining parameters refitted at
each value, moves \(R^{2}\) only from 0.746 to 0.755 as \(d_{1}\) rises from
10 to 200 MGy, and resampling the film positions places \(d_{1}\) anywhere
between 0.16 and 200 MGy. Fits
traversing less than half of their modelled decay are flagged as lower bounds
throughout, and no fitted curve is drawn for them.

A second exponential improves the description of every trace, raising
\(R^{2}\) to 0.993 or above and lowering the Akaike information criterion by
several hundred, but it was not adopted. Bootstrapped over film positions the
slow component is unconstrained, spanning 0.46 to 200 MGy at 5 \% transmission
and reaching the fitting bound in three resamples in ten. The gain is in
describing a single realisation rather than in estimating a second rate that
would replicate, and with five positions per condition a single exponential with
an explicit identifiability criterion is the more defensible summary.

The subtraction is not cosmetic. Taken alone, the 412 nm trace of the labelled
film is not monotonic: it falls to an extremum within the first few MGy and then
returns partway towards its starting value, by 11 \% of the fall at 5 \%
transmission and 76 \% at 25 \%. That recovery is neither a return of the label
nor a detector artefact, since no spectrometer resets are recorded in that
series. It is the red tail of the protein absorbance growth centred near 310 nm
encroaching on the 412 nm window as that band builds, and over the recovering
segment the two are correlated at \(r = +0.96\) while the 470--500 nm internal
zero changes by less than 0.001. The growth is common to both soak states, so it
cancels in the difference, which is monotonic to within 5 \% and is fitted over
its full range.
The growth at 310 and 328 nm behaves in the opposite way, its fitted
\(D_{90}\) falling at 73 to 94 \% of the measured dose range in every long
condition, so that the characteristic dose there is a lower bound set by the
point at which the film failed optically rather than a property of the chemistry.
For comparison, \textcite{sutton2013insights} report \(D_{90}\) at 400 nm
averaging 0.51 to 0.77 MGy in lysozyme.

Rate constants are not quoted. Bootstrapped over film positions the fitted decay
constant at 5 \% transmission spans two orders of magnitude, and a global test of
whether a single rate describes all four conditions or whether each requires its
own returned one negative rate together with an improvement in information
criterion of only 1.2 \% in residual sum of squares; shared and independent rates
are thus indistinguishable in these data. What can be stated is that the loss is
not adequately described by a single exponential over the whole range, the trace
returning by 11 \% of its fall at 5 \% transmission and by 76 \% at 25 \%. Part
of that recovery coincides with the dose range in which the internal null drifts
most, and it should not presently be interpreted as chemistry.

Two observations constrain the mechanism. First, the 412 nm difference is negative
from the first analysed frame and becomes only more negative; at no dose in any
condition does it rise. Release of free TNB\(^{2-}\) into the probed volume would
increase absorbance at 412 nm, so the data are consistent with destruction of the
chromophore or with its loss from the probed volume, and not with accumulation of
the released ion. Whether the chromophore is destroyed in place or released and
then lost by lateral diffusion out of the probe footprint cannot be distinguished
by this measurement. Second, the process requires X-rays: in a DTNB soaked film
recorded with the shutter closed the scatter corrected TNB window signal is flat
to within 0.001 absorbance units over 20 s, whereas irradiated films have lost
between 0.019 and 0.032 over the same interval. Spontaneous decay, thermal
relaxation and photobleaching by the probe beam are therefore all excluded as
explanations. Mother liquor alone, irradiated under the same conditions, likewise
produces no signal of its own, remaining within 0.0022 absorbance units at
300--325 nm and 0.0006 at 395--430 nm over 26 s (Figure \ref{fig:spec_buffer}).

The direction of these observations is consistent with the established picture of
specific radiation damage, in which disulphide bonds are among the first sites to
be affected, cleaving by capture of photoelectrons and solvated electrons
generated in the surrounding solvent
\parencite{weik2000specific, burmeister2000structural, garman2010radiation}. A
disulphide radical anion absorbing near 400 nm has been observed by
\textit{in crystallo} spectroscopy during irradiation
\parencite{sutton2013insights}, and different disulphides within one protein are
known to cleave at different rates \parencite{weik2002specific}. It is therefore
plausible that the mixed protein--S--S--TNB disulphide introduced by DTNB labelling
is cleaved by the same route, releasing the TNB moiety, which is then lost from
the probed volume; the observations above are consistent with that picture but do
not establish it, since neither the radical intermediate nor the released ion is
separately resolved here.

The response at 100 K is markedly attenuated (Figure \ref{fig:spec_cryo}). In the
single DTNB soaked crystal measured at 100 K the integrated 395--430 nm signal
remains at \(+0.002\) through two successive X-ray exposures, rises to
\(+0.005\) after the third and to \(+0.020\) at the fourth and unattenuated
exposure, in contrast to the negative excursion reached at room temperature.
Only at the final, unattenuated exposure does the cryocooled crystal depart
appreciably from its starting state. The comparison is necessarily qualitative,
since the cryocooled measurements were made on single crystals with an exposure
index rather than a calibrated dose axis, and only one DTNB soaked crystal was
measured; nevertheless the direction is consistent with the suppression of
secondary radiation chemistry below the solvent glass transition, where the
diffusion of radiolytic species is greatly restricted
\parencite{garman2010radiation}.

An unexpected feature of the room temperature data is that the loss superimposes
more closely when plotted against elapsed time than against absorbed dose. Across
a twentyfold range of dose rate the spread between conditions at matched dose is
2.6 to 4.5 fold, whereas at matched time it is 1.7 to 2.7 fold. Since the
no X-ray control establishes that nothing happens without irradiation, the
process is X-ray initiated but appears partly limited by a time dependent step,
which would be expected if diffusion of a radiolytic species, or of the released
TNB out of the probe footprint, were rate limiting. An inverse dose rate effect
of this kind has precedent at room temperature, where crystals tolerate a larger
total dose when it is delivered more rapidly
\parencite{owen2012outrunning}. This interpretation should
be treated as tentative: the dose axis itself carries the shutter timing
uncertainty described above, and a systematic error in the recovered onset would
act in the same direction.

Taken together these observations indicate that the TNB label is lost from the
crystal under X-ray irradiation at room temperature, and they permit a first
estimate of the dose budget for a combined diffraction and spectroscopy
experiment (Figure \ref{fig:spec_budget}). The dose at which the label specific
difference first exceeds the measured baseline floor of 0.004 absorbance units
is 0.03, 0.06, 0.09 and 0.24 MGy at 5, 25, 50 and 100 \% transmission. A
linear extrapolation from the initial slope, which is the more conservative
basis for planning because it does not rely on the sharply convex early part of
the response, instead gives 0.24, 0.29, 0.45 and 0.79 MGy. Room temperature
diffraction lifetimes for comparable systems span roughly 0.10 to 0.37 MGy
depending on protein and collection speed \parencite{owen2012outrunning}, so on
the conservative basis the measurement requires between about two thirds and
three times the dose a single crystal survives at the lowest dose rate, rising to
between two and eight times at the highest. Detection within the lifetime of one
crystal is thus marginal at best, and only at low dose rate; averaging of order
four crystals brings the low dose rate case comfortably within budget, whereas
the fastest collection would require of order ten. Two practical conclusions
follow. Watching the label leave during a diffraction experiment is feasible but
must be fast, and the multi-position film geometry used here, in which the
crystalline volume fraction varies severalfold between positions, is poorly
suited to it; large single crystals under cryocooling, where the label survives,
are the appropriate configuration for the online spectroscopy that such an
experiment would require. A room temperature multicrystal implementation remains
some way off.

A caveat applies to all of the above. The internal null window at 470--500 nm,
which should remain at zero once the scattering background has been removed,
instead reads \(-0.0026\) to \(-0.0040\) absorbance units at the last analysed
frame in the DTNB conditions, with a position to position standard deviation of
0.0013 to 0.0029. This sets the baseline floor at approximately 0.003 to 0.004
absorbance units; the endpoint TNB window difference of 0.015 to 0.039 stands
between six and thirteen times above it. The magnitude of the TNB signal is
additionally sensitive to the assumed scattering exponent, shifting by 11 to
60 \% depending on condition when the exponent is varied between 1 and 4. These
systematic effects bound the precision of the values reported here, although they
are considerably smaller than the difference between the labelled and unlabelled
films, and do not affect the sign of that difference, on which the principal
result rests.
